Vehicle Emissions
On pages 90 and 107 the draft EIS states that by the time the airport spur is open to traffic, the vehicles using it will be subject to stringent government regulations. This statement is inaccurate because the federal emission limits originally set for 1975 and now postponed until 1976 will apply only to 1976 and later model-year cars. There will still be many older cars on the highways and there is no requirement presently anticipated for retrofitting them with comparable emission control devices. Earlier model-year cars made in the mid 1970's will presumably have control devices designed to bring them into compliance with interim emission standards. However it remains to be seen how reliable the new devices are and how rapidly they deteriorate from their original operating efficiency.
The possibility of further easing of federal emission control regulations or enforcement schedules should also be taken into account. The questions of how soon cars meeting the 1976 standards will actually be available and whether they will in fact maintain the required emission control for 50,000 miles remain in some doubt. In view of these considerations, the EPA prediction of a 25% reduction in carbon monoxide emissions by 1975, mentioned on page 90 of the statement, should be considered highly optimistic.
The emission factors given on page 92 of the statement and used in the calculations on pages 92B and 92C will underrate the emissions from Wisconsin cars because they are based on California cars. California law has predated federal law in requiring increasingly strict emission controls on automobiles. (This does not invalidate the corridor comparisons made on page 92B, however). In addition, the accuracy of any predicted future emission rates depends on the validity of the assumption that planned federal regulations will be successfully implemented and firmly enforced. A more sound approach to predicting emission rates along a new freeway such as the airport spur might be to collect data on the actual trends in emissions along present Milwaukee freeways as emission controlled vehicles come into wider use. These data could then be used to determine the actual improvements to be expected when future vehicle emission regulations go into effect.
Development Which Generates New Traffic
The draft EIS gives projections showing total passenger and aircraft movement at General Mitchell Field more than doubling before 1990. In planning for this sort of rapid expansion, the fact that patterns of development in urban areas can have a marked impact on air quality needs to be taken into account.
